Local utilities

Local utilities with no connection or network, decoding a JWT, inventorying dependencies from manifests and lockfiles, checked encoding and hashing, decoding certificates and checking a chain, summarising test, SARIF and coverage reports, triaging a large log, scanning for secrets before a commit or post, sizing files and folders before reading them, time zone, duration, business-day and cron arithmetic, comparing versions and ranges for npm, NuGet and Maven, and converting Markdown to and from Jira and Confluence formats

Docs / Local utilities

Group
toil util
Credential
None
Network
None

skills/toil/util.md

Commands that work on what’s on this machine: a token or version you paste, a file or folder in the workspace (a certificate or a log, say), the manifests and lockfiles there, a report a build left behind, text you’re about to commit or post, or a time and a time zone. They aren’t integrations. There is no server, no connection to add, no TOIL_UTIL_* variable, no credential and no --connection flag, and none of them sends anything over the network. None changes anything: the only file one writes is a new one you name with --out, inside the workspace, and it never replaces a file. Verification level: unit.

jwt and deps also have a short path, an alias that does the same thing with the same flags and output:

toil util jwt decodetoil jwt decodeutil_jwt_decode
toil util deps scantoil deps scanutil_deps_scan

Over MCP the tools are served without any configuration. toil mcp --areas util serves just these.

By job

The same commands, grouped by what you need them for.

Reading CI output

What a build or a scanner leaves behind, turned into something short enough to read: totals and failures from a report, and the errors that matter from a log thousands of lines long.

  • Summarising a report (toil util report): Turns what CI and scanners write into one JSON summary. JUnit XML (Maven Surefire, Jenkins and Azure DevOps shapes) and TRX become test totals plus each failure with its suite, name, file, line, message and the first lines of its stack. SARIF 2.1.0 becomes findings with rule, level, file and line. lcov and Cobertura become per-file line and branch percentages and the lowest-covered files.
  • Triaging a log (toil util log): Reads a CI console, a Maven, npm or dotnet build, or a test run, and returns what’s worth reading: the error and warning lines grouped by signature, with numbers, ids, timestamps and hex replaced so the same complaint counts once. Each group has its count, its first and last line, one sample, and the Java, .NET, Node or Python stack trace that belongs to it.

Writing for the tools

Getting text into the shape an enterprise tool expects before it’s sent, so a description, a page or a request arrives the way it was meant.

  • Converting Markdown (toil util md): Turns Markdown into Jira wiki markup (Jira Data Center), Atlassian Document Format (Jira Cloud and Confluence Cloud) or Confluence storage format (Confluence Data Center), and any of those back into Markdown.

Safety

Checks to run before something leaves the machine or gets trusted: a secret in a diff, a certificate chain that won’t validate, a token’s claims, and the dependencies a repository ships.

  • Scanning for secrets (toil util secrets scan): Looks for credential-shaped strings before you commit, push or post them: tokens, keys, password= values, credentials in URLs, private keys and long random strings. It uses the same rules toil’s audit log redacts with, plus an entropy check, and exits with 1 when it finds anything, so a hook or a pipeline can stop on it.
  • Decoding certificates (toil util cert): Decodes a certificate or a chain bundle, PEM or DER: subject, issuer, SANs, serial, how many days it has left, its key, its signature algorithm, its basic constraints and key usage, and its fingerprints, so a TLS failure can be explained from the files. It never connects to the host.
  • Decoding a JWT (toil util jwt decode): Shows a token’s header and claims, so you can see who it’s for, what it grants and when it expires.
  • Inventorying dependencies (toil util deps scan, toil util deps diff): deps scan lists every package the workspace’s npm, NuGet and Maven/Gradle manifests and lockfiles declare, with its version, the file it came from, and whether it’s direct or transitive, production or dev. That inventory is what the vulnerability and licence commands read, one source per command, so you choose which service sees your dependency list. deps diff lists what was added, removed, upgraded or downgraded between two git refs.

Arithmetic models get wrong

Work that looks simple and is easy to get subtly wrong by reasoning alone: time zones and DST, version ordering, encodings and hashes, and how big a file is before reading it. Each one works the answer out, then checks it a second way.

  • Time zones, durations, business days and cron (toil util time convert, toil util time duration, toil util time business-days add, toil util time business-days diff, toil util time cron): Date arithmetic on the time zone data Node already ships: convert a time between zones, read or write an ISO 8601 duration, add or count business days, and list a cron schedule’s next run times.
  • Comparing versions (toil util semver compare, toil util semver satisfies, toil util semver sort, toil util semver bump): Compare, sort and bump versions, and check them against ranges, in the grammar of the ecosystem they come from: npm (SemVer 2.0.0 and npm’s ranges, the default), NuGet (up to four parts, interval notation) or Maven (Maven’s own ordering, where 1.0.0.Final is 1 and SNAPSHOT comes before the release).
  • Encoding, decoding and hashing (toil util encode): Base64, base64url, hex, URL components and form values, in either direction, and a file’s SHA-256, SHA-1 or MD5 hash.
  • Sizing before reading (toil util size): Tells an agent how much a file or folder will cost to read. For a file it gives bytes, lines, an estimated token count, and an outline: functions, classes and methods with their line ranges for TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, C#, Java and Go, headings for Markdown, and top-level keys for JSON and YAML, so the agent reads only the lines it needs. For a folder it gives a tree of totals, largest first, and names the largest files.

Commands

toil util jwt decode

Decodes a JWT’s header and claims without verifying it. There’s no key and no network call, and nothing here says whether the token is valid, expired or trusted.

toil util jwt decode eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJhYmMxMjM0NSJ9.c2ln
echo "$TOKEN" | toil util jwt decode -
ArgumentMeaning
<token>The token, header.payload.signature. - reads it from stdin, which keeps it out of the process list and your shell history; one trailing line ending is dropped

Output: { header, payload, signature }, the header and claims as parsed JSON and the signature segment as the text it is.

  • A token that isn’t three dot-separated parts (an encrypted 5-part JWE, say) fails with INVALID_INPUT, Invalid JWT: expected 3 dot-separated parts.
  • A header or payload that doesn’t decode to JSON fails with Invalid JWT: header is not valid JSON (or payload). A Bearer prefix gives this error too, so strip it.
  • The decoding is lenient, as it has always been. A segment that is JSON but not an object (null, a number) comes back as it is. Characters outside base64url are skipped. Invalid UTF-8 shows as �. Whitespace in a token passed as an argument is kept, so a trailing newline ends up in signature.

The token goes nowhere but the decoder. toil doesn’t log it, and no error message repeats it.

toil util deps scan

The dependency inventory of the workspace, from its manifests and lockfiles. It reads files only and needs no git. It must be inside a git repository, though, or it fails with Not inside a git repository. deps commands require a git repo root.

toil util deps scan
toil util deps scan --ecosystem npm --include-transitive --include-dev
toil util deps scan | toil osv vulns
FlagMeaning
--ecosystem <ecosystem>npm, nuget, maven or all (default). Any other value matches nothing and scans nothing
--include-transitiveInclude transitive dependencies (left out by default)
--include-devInclude dev and test dependencies (left out by default)

Which files it reads:

  • Which files: every file in the workspace that git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard would list. That’s tracked files plus untracked ones .gitignore and .git/info/exclude don’t cover. A nested repository isn’t walked into. Your global git excludes file isn’t read, so a file only it ignores is scanned.
  • npm: package.json (not under node_modules), with the first of package-lock.json (v2 or later), yarn.lock (v1) or pnpm-lock.yaml beside it. A package-lock.json with no packages falls back to package.json.
  • NuGet: .csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj, packages.config and Directory.Packages.props, with a packages.lock.json in the same folder. Project files that share one lock file count once. A project with no version on a PackageReference takes it from the nearest Directory.Packages.props, up to 10 folders up.
  • Maven/Gradle: pom.xml, build.gradle and build.gradle.kts, with a gradle.lockfile beside them.

A lockfile wins over its manifest. Packages are de-duplicated on ecosystem, name, version and source file. A manifest that can’t be read is skipped. One that exists but can’t be read (a link out of the workspace, say) also gets a DEPS_FILE_SKIPPED warning in meta.warnings. That warning is the only check it makes of its own result: the deps commands have no verified block, so treat the quirks below as unchecked.

Output:

{
  "ecosystems": ["npm", "nuget", "maven"],
  "manifests": [{ "file": "package.json", "ecosystem": "npm", "lockFile": "package-lock.json" }],
  "packages": [{ "name": "lodash", "version": "4.17.21", "ecosystem": "npm", "source": "package-lock.json", "type": "direct", "scope": "production" }],
  "summary": { "totalPackages": 1, "byEcosystem": { "npm": 1 }, "byType": { "direct": 1, "transitive": 0 }, "byScope": { "production": 1, "dev": 0 } }
}

Paths are relative to the workspace, with forward slashes. Maven names are group:artifact. When the repository’s root is above the workspace, only the workspace is scanned: run it from the root, or pass --workspace <root>, to scan everything.

Known quirks, which stay until they’re checked against real repositories:

  • In an npm v7+ lockfile, direct means hoisted to the top node_modules, so most transitive packages count as direct. Workspace folders show up as packages.
  • Yarn 1 headers with several ranges give a garbled name. Yarn 2+ lockfiles give no packages.
  • pnpm peer suffixes stay in the version, and pnpm 9’s scoped packages are missed.
  • CentralTransitive NuGet packages count as direct.
  • gradle.lockfile test dependencies are always included.
  • Any word 'a:b:c' string in build.gradle reads as a dependency.
  • pom.xml plugin dependencies count as the project’s.

The output is the inventory the vulnerability and licence commands read from stdin or --from <file>: toil osv vulns, toil ossindex vulns, toil sonatypeiq evaluate, and toil artifactory outdated / license-check. Over MCP, save it to a file in the workspace and pass that file’s path as from.

toil util deps diff

How the inventory changed between two git refs. This command runs the git on PATH: git ls-tree for each ref’s files and git show for each one it reads. Without git it fails with GIT_NOT_FOUND.

toil util deps diff --from main
toil util deps diff --from v1.0.0 --to main --ecosystem npm --include-dev
FlagMeaning
--from <ref>The base ref: a commit, tag or branch. Required
--to <ref>The target ref (default: the working tree, scanned as deps scan does)
--ecosystem <ecosystem>npm, nuget, maven or all (default)
--include-devInclude dev and test dependencies

Transitive dependencies are always included. Output: { from, to, changes: [{ name, ecosystem, change, from, to, source }], summary: { added, removed, upgraded, downgraded, unchanged } }. change is added, removed, upgraded or downgraded. Unchanged packages are counted, not listed. to reads working tree when --to is left out.

Known quirks:

  • A ref git can’t read (a typo, or one you haven’t fetched) gives an empty inventory for that side, so a bad --from reports every package as added. Check the ref first.
  • Each package is keyed on ecosystem, name and source file, and one version per key survives. A package present at two versions can show a change that didn’t happen.
  • Paths that git quotes (non-ASCII names) aren’t read at a ref.
  • A ref that starts with -, or an empty --from, is refused with INVALID_INPUT before git runs. An empty --to means the working tree.

toil util secrets scan

Finds credential-shaped strings before an agent or a person commits, pushes, comments or posts them. It reads a file, a folder, stdin, text, or the repository’s staged or working-tree diff, and talks to nothing.

toil util secrets scan --diff staged          # before git commit
toil util secrets scan src/                   # a folder, .gitignore respected
toil util secrets scan notes.md
gh pr view 12 --json body -q .body | toil util secrets scan -
toil util secrets scan --text "$COMMENT"
Argument / flagMeaning
[path]A file or folder inside the workspace. A folder is walked as git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard would list it. -, or nothing at all, reads stdin
--text <text>The content itself, instead of a file
--diff <kind>staged scans what the next commit holds (git diff --staged); working scans unstaged changes (git diff). Added lines only, in the workspace only. Runs the git on PATH
--allow-file <file>The allow file (default: .toil/secrets-allow at the workspace’s top, when it exists)

Pass one of a path, --text or --diff; two at once is INVALID_INPUT. Over MCP, pass file, text or diff.

The exit code is 1 when anything is found, and 0 when nothing is, so a hook or a pipeline can gate on it. The envelope stays ok: true either way; ok: false (also exit 1) means the scan itself failed.

What it looks for:

  • The rules the audit log redacts with, so toil has one definition of a secret: GitHub, GitLab, Slack, AWS, SonarQube, sk- and Atlassian tokens, JWTs, private keys, credentials in URLs, Bearer / Basic / Token values, name=value pairs whose name says secret (password=, "apiToken":, --token=), curl -u user:pass, and long random runs of letters and digits.
  • high-entropy: a run of 20 or more base64 or base64url characters, holding letters and digits, that those rules didn’t catch and whose Shannon entropy is at least 4.2 bits per character.

Two things are set aside and counted instead of reported: Subresource Integrity checksums (sha512-… in lockfiles, counted in summary.checksums), and a named value that is a reference to a secret rather than one (token: ${{ secrets.X }}, password=$DB_PASSWORD, <your-token>, xxx, counted in summary.placeholders). Commits, digests and UUIDs aren’t findings.

Output:

{
  "source": { "kind": "staged", "path": null },
  "findings": [{ "file": "config/application.properties", "line": 4, "column": 28, "length": 14, "rule": "name-value", "confidence": "high", "entropy": 3.18, "preview": "…", "fingerprint": "e594506f-49ad270a-55b41205-70d9b059" }],
  "allowed": [],
  "unreadable": [{ "file": "logo.png", "reason": "binary", "message": "logo.png is binary in the diff; its content wasn't scanned." }],
  "allowList": null,
  "summary": { "files": 1, "lines": 5, "findings": 1, "allowed": 0, "unreadable": 1, "checksums": 0, "placeholders": 0, "byRule": { "name-value": 1 } },
  "verified": { "passed": true, "checks": [] }
}
  • file is relative to the workspace, with forward slashes, or null for stdin and text. line and column start at 1; columns count UTF-16 code units. A private key spanning lines is one finding, with endLine.
  • source.kind is file, folder, stdin, text, staged or working.
  • confidence is high for a vendor’s token format, high or medium for a value a name or scheme marks as secret (medium when it’s short and plain), and graded by entropy for a random run (low below 3.5 bits per character).
  • The full secret is never in the output, nor in a warning, an error or the audit log, which keeps no copy of text. preview keeps at most 4 characters at each end of a secret of 24 or more, 2 of one of 16 to 23, and none of a shorter one: ghp_…c9vB, ….
  • fingerprint identifies the value without revealing it: a salted scrypt, four groups of 8 hex digits. It’s slow on purpose, so a short password can’t be recovered from it by guessing at speed.

The allow file lists known false positives, one fingerprint per line, copied from a finding. # starts a comment. It’s matched by fingerprint only, never by the raw value, so it’s safe to check in. A finding it names goes in allowed instead of findings and doesn’t set the exit code. allowList says which file was read, how many entries it had, how many lines weren’t fingerprints, and how many entries matched nothing. A line that isn’t a fingerprint is ignored with a SECRETS_ALLOW_INVALID warning that gives its line number and never its text. A named --allow-file that doesn’t exist is INVALID_INPUT.

# .toil/secrets-allow
e594506f-49ad270a-55b41205-70d9b059  # the test fixture's dummy password

What it checks of its own result (verified):

  • finding.reread: every finding is read again at its reported line, from the file on disk, from the index (git show :<path>) for a staged diff, or from what stdin or the text held. The same characters must be at the same column, with the same rule finding them. A mismatch warns SECRETS_REREAD_MISMATCH.
  • preview.masked: every preview is checked to hold none of the secret’s middle. One that fails warns SECRETS_PREVIEW_LEAK and is replaced by ….
  • input.complete: each file was read to its size on disk. For a diff this is unchecked, with an UNVERIFIED warning, since git’s output has no size to compare with; the re-read checks each finding instead.

What it couldn’t read is listed, never skipped silently. unreadable holds each binary file, each file over 64 MiB, each one it couldn’t open (a permission error, say), each nested repository a folder scan didn’t walk into, and each line over 4 MiB, of which only the start was scanned. Any of them adds a SECRETS_UNREADABLE warning. A single file named on the call that can’t be read is an INVALID_INPUT error instead. --diff working also warns SECRETS_UNTRACKED_NOT_SCANNED with the number of untracked files, which no diff holds: scan the folder, or stage them, to include them.

A diff covers the workspace, not the whole repository. When the workspace is a folder inside the repository, changes outside it aren’t scanned, and a SECRETS_DIFF_PARTIAL warning gives the number of changed files left out. To check a whole commit, run it with --workspace at the repository’s top.

Known limits:

  • A diff and a file are scanned line by line, so a secret split across two lines (other than a private key) isn’t found.
  • A private key spans lines only when its BEGIN line stands alone and an END line follows its body (base64, blank, Proc-Type: and DEK-Info: lines). It’s then one finding, with endLine. When no END comes (another line, a gap between diff hunks, or the end of the file), the BEGIN line is reported on its own and the lines below it are scanned as usual.
  • A bare key= isn’t treated as a secret’s name, because in toil’s inputs it’s an issue, space or project key. A real key there is still caught by its shape or its entropy.

toil util encode

Encodes or decodes base64, base64url, hex and URL percent-encoding, and hashes a file with SHA-256, SHA-1 or MD5. Each result is checked before it’s returned, and data.verified says how.

toil util encode base64 --text 'you@example.com:abc12345'
toil util encode base64 --decode mail-part.b64 --out logo.png
toil util encode url --text 'project = PAY AND assignee = "you@example.com"'
toil util encode form --decode --text 'project+%3D+PAY+AND+assignee+%3D+%22you%40example.com%22'
printf 'hello' | toil util encode hex
toil util encode sha256 release.tgz
Argument or flagMeaning
<scheme>base64, base64url, hex, url, form, or a hash: sha256, sha1, md5. Required
[file]A file inside the workspace. -, or leaving out both the file and --text, reads stdin
--text <text>The content itself, instead of a file. It’s encoded as UTF-8
--decodeDecode instead of encode. Not for a hash
--out <file>Write the result to this new file inside the workspace instead of returning it. Never replaces a file. Not for a hash

The schemes:

  • base64 is written padded. Decoding accepts it with or without padding, and ignores spaces and line breaks, so MIME-wrapped base64 reads as it is.
  • base64url (- and _) is written without padding, as JWTs use it, and read with or without.
  • hex is written in lower case and read in either. Spaces and line breaks are ignored; a 0x prefix or : separators are not.
  • url is a URL component, written as JavaScript’s encodeURIComponent writes it: letters, digits and -_.!~*'() stay, every other byte becomes %XX.
  • form is one name or value of an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body: letters, digits and *-._ stay, a space becomes +, and every other byte becomes %XX. Decode a body one field at a time. A whole body decodes, but its = and & come back the same as an encoded %3D and %26, so roundtrip.encode fails, as it should.

Output:

  • Encode: { operation: "encode", scheme, inputBytes, outputBytes, output, verified }.
  • Decode: { operation: "decode", scheme, inputBytes, outputBytes, utf8, output, verified }. utf8 says whether the decoded bytes are valid UTF-8.
  • Hash: { operation: "hash", scheme, inputBytes, hex, base64, verified }, the digest both ways.
  • With --out, file (the absolute path written) replaces output.

The input is bytes: a file or stdin is encoded or hashed exactly as it is, so echo hello | toil util encode base64 includes the newline echo adds. Use printf or --text to leave it out. When decoding, one trailing line ending is dropped.

Decoded bytes that aren’t valid UTF-8 are refused with INVALID_INPUT unless --out names a file to write them to. JSON can only carry them as text, and any text would be different bytes. Valid UTF-8 comes back as the text it is.

What data.verified checks:

CheckWhat it means
roundtrip.decodeAn encode was decoded back, and gave exactly the input
roundtrip.encodeA decode was encoded again, and gave the input, allowing for whitespace, padding, the case of hex and %XX, and %20 for + in a form
input.completeThe bytes read equal the file’s size on disk, so a read that stopped short can’t pass. Unchecked for stdin, which has no size
output.fileThe file written was read back, and holds exactly the bytes written

A failed check sets verified.passed to false and adds a warning: ENCODE_ROUNDTRIP_MISMATCH, INPUT_INCOMPLETE or ENCODE_OUTPUT_MISMATCH. Input that decodes but fails roundtrip.encode isn’t how the scheme writes those bytes. For example, base64 QR== decodes to A, but base64 writes A as QQ==, and a URL with a space left in it isn’t encoded. Check that it wasn’t changed on the way.

Errors:

  • Text that isn’t the scheme is INVALID_INPUT, naming the offset of the first character that’s wrong but never the character, in case the text is a credential. A base64 character that only base64url uses (or the other way round) says to try the other scheme.
  • A file to decode that looks binary (a NUL byte), --decode or --out with a hash, and a scheme toil doesn’t have are INVALID_INPUT.
  • Encoding or decoding reads at most 64 MiB. A hash of a file streams, with no limit; stdin is held in memory, so it keeps the 64 MiB limit.

MD5 and SHA-1 are here to match checksums that other tools publish, not to protect anything. The audit log keeps only a hash of --text.

toil util cert

Decodes X.509 certificates, one or a chain bundle, in PEM or DER, so you can explain a TLS failure from the files. It never connects to the host the certificate is for: pass the file the server is configured with, or the chain a client saved.

toil util cert chain.pem
toil util cert chain.pem --host api.imagile.dev
toil util cert server.der
cat chain.pem | toil util cert -
Argument or flagMeaning
[file]A file in the workspace, PEM or DER. -, or leaving it out, reads stdin
--text <text>The PEM itself, instead of a file. Over MCP, text is read as UTF-8, so a DER certificate goes as file
--host <host>A host name or IP address: do the first certificate’s SANs cover it?

Output: { format, certificates, skipped, chain, host, verified }. Each certificate is { position, line, offset, subject, issuer, sans, serial, validity: { notBefore, notAfter, daysLeft, status }, key: { type, bits, curve }, signatureAlgorithm: { name, oid }, selfSigned, basicConstraints: { ca, pathLength }, keyUsage, extendedKeyUsage, fingerprints: { sha1, sha256 } }. position counts every block in a PEM bundle (or element in a DER one) from 1, line is where a PEM block starts and offset where a DER certificate does. status is valid, expired or not-yet-valid, and daysLeft is negative once expired. basicConstraints, keyUsage and extendedKeyUsage are null when the certificate doesn’t have that extension.

What it checks, in data.verified (a failure also warns under its code):

CheckMeansFails with
bundle.readableEvery block meant to be a certificate decodesCERT_UNREADABLE
decode.matchesNodetoil’s DER reader and node:crypto agree on the serial and CA flag, and nothing follows the certificate in its blockCERT_DECODE_MISMATCH
validity.notExpired, validity.startedEach certificate is inside its validity window nowCERT_EXPIRED, CERT_NOT_YET_VALID
chain.orderEach certificate’s issuer is the next one’s subjectCERT_CHAIN_ORDER
chain.signatureWhere the names match, each signature verifies with the next certificate’s key, and a self-issued last certificate with its ownCERT_SIGNATURE_MISMATCH
chain.rootUnchecked (UNVERIFIED) when the last certificate isn’t self-signed, so its issuer doesn’t follow it: the chain is checked only as far as the bundle goes
host.coveredWith --host, a DNS or IP SAN of the first certificate covers itCERT_HOST_MISMATCH
input.completeThe whole file was read (unchecked for stdin)INPUT_INCOMPLETE
  • The chain is checked in the order given, leaf first. When it’s out of order but is one chain in another order, chain.suggestedOrder lists the positions in the right order and CERT_CHAIN_REORDER says so.
  • chain.inOrder is true when every link’s names match and every signature checked verifies. chain.root is included when the last certificate is self-signed. Nothing is checked against a trust store: a chain that verifies to a root in the bundle isn’t thereby trusted.
  • --host follows what browsers do: SANs only, never the subject CN, and a wildcard covers exactly one label (*.imagile.dev covers api.imagile.dev, not imagile.dev or a.api.imagile.dev). host.explanation says why it’s covered or not.
  • A PEM block that isn’t a certificate is skipped, listed in skipped and named in a CERT_BLOCK_SKIPPED warning. A private key is never read, and CERT_PRIVATE_KEY_IN_INPUT says one was there. CERTIFICATE and X509 CERTIFICATE blocks are read; TRUSTED CERTIFICATE, PKCS#7 (.p7b) and PKCS#12 (.pfx) are not.
  • In DER input a damaged certificate ends the reading, since nothing says where the next one starts; it’s reported at its byte offset.
  • Input with no certificate that can be read fails with INVALID_INPUT, naming each block and why.

toil util semver

Versions and ranges in the grammar of the ecosystem they come from. Pick it with --ecosystem: npm (the default), nuget or maven.

  • npm: SemVer 2.0.0 versions (1.2.3, 1.2.3-rc.1+build.5; a leading v is allowed) and npm’s ranges, as package.json takes them: ^1.2.3, ~1.2, 1.x, >=1.0.0 <2.0.0, 1.0.0 - 2.0.0, joined with ||. A prerelease satisfies a range only when the range names a prerelease of the same major.minor.patch, unless you pass --include-prerelease. There’s no loose mode that turns text that isn’t a version into one.
  • nuget: one to four numbers (1, 1.0 and 1.0.0.0 are one version), then an optional -prerelease and +metadata. Labels compare case-insensitively. Ranges are interval notation: 1.0 (at least 1.0), [1.0], [1.0,2.0), (,2.0]. A prerelease inside the bounds satisfies the range. Floating versions (1.*, 1.0.0-*) are refused, because what one picks depends on the feed.
  • maven: Maven’s own ordering: alpha < beta < milestone < rc < snapshot < release < sp, 1, 1.0 and 1.0.0.Final are one version, and 1a1 is 1-alpha-1. A version is letters, digits, ., -, _ and + with at least one digit, so an unresolved ${property} is reported, not ordered. Ranges are [1.0,2.0), [1.0] and (,1.0],[1.2,). A bare version is a soft requirement that any version satisfies, and says so in a MAVEN_SOFT_REQUIREMENT warning.

A version or range that doesn’t parse in the chosen grammar is INVALID_INPUT, with the reason and an example of what fits. Build metadata never affects order.

toil util semver compare 1.0.0-rc.10 1.0.0-rc.9
toil util semver satisfies 1.3.0-rc.1 '^1.2.0' --include-prerelease
toil util semver satisfies 5.3.39 '[5.0,6.0)' --ecosystem maven
toil util semver sort versions.txt --range '^5.0.0'
toil util semver bump 1.2.3 prerelease --preid rc
CommandArguments and flagsOutput
compare <a> <b>--ecosystem <ecosystem>{ ecosystem, a, b, order, higher, difference, normalized: { a, b }, verified }. order is -1, 0 or 1 for a against b, higher is a, b or null, and difference is the most significant part they differ in: major, minor, patch, revision (NuGet’s fourth part, or Maven’s), prerelease, qualifier (Maven) or null
satisfies <version> <range>--ecosystem <ecosystem>, --include-prerelease{ ecosystem, version, range, normalizedRange, satisfies, verified }
sort [file]--text <text>, --ecosystem <ecosystem>, --range <range>, --include-prerelease{ ecosystem, count, sorted, invalid, verified }, lowest first, plus { range, normalizedRange, satisfying, highest } with --range
bump <version> <release>--ecosystem <ecosystem>, --preid <id>{ ecosystem, version, release, preid, result, verified }
  • sort reads a file in the workspace, stdin (-, or no file), or --text. Versions go one per line or separated by spaces. An entry that doesn’t parse is left out of the sort and listed in invalid with its line and the reason, with a SEMVER_INVALID_VERSION warning.
  • bump takes major, minor or patch in every ecosystem. npm also takes premajor, preminor, prepatch, prerelease and release, the bumps npm publishes with, and --preid names the prerelease (1.2.3 prerelease --preid rc is 1.2.4-rc.0). A NuGet result has three parts, with the revision and labels dropped. Maven bumps the leading numbers and drops the qualifier (1.2.3-SNAPSHOT minor is 1.3.0).

What it checks (verified, with failures as warnings):

  • sort.transitive: every pair in the sorted list is in order, so a comparison where a < b and b < c but not a < c can’t hide. Up to 2,000 versions; past that, each against its neighbour, reported as APPROXIMATED.
  • sort.antisymmetric, sort.complete: each neighbouring pair compares the same both ways round, and every entry is either sorted or listed as invalid.
  • range.boundaries, range.answers: each answer agrees with the range’s intervals, worked out by comparison alone, at the range’s boundary versions and at every version asked about. A range with no bounds (*) has none to test, and says so with UNVERIFIED.
  • compare.antisymmetric, diff.consistent, bump.increases, version.normalized: b against a is the reverse of a against b, a difference is named exactly when the versions differ, a bump goes up, and a normalised version reads back as the same version.
  • input.complete: the whole file was read. stdin has no size to compare with, so it’s UNVERIFIED.

diff names the most significant part that changed, the same rule in every ecosystem; it never answers premajor or the like.

toil util report

One JSON summary of a report that CI or a scanner wrote: JUnit XML, TRX, SARIF 2.1.0, lcov or Cobertura. It reads the file and nothing else, and checks the report against its own declared totals.

toil util report target/surefire-reports/TEST-dev.imagile.OrderTest.xml
toil util report TestResults/build.trx
toil util report coverage/lcov.info --lowest 5
toil util report results.sarif
cat coverage.xml | toil util report --format cobertura
Argument / flagMeaning
[file]The report, inside the workspace. -, or no file and no --text, reads stdin
--text <text>The report itself, instead of a file
--format <format>junit, trx, sarif, lcov or cobertura. Left out, it’s detected from the content: the root element for XML (<testsuites> or <testsuite>, <TestRun>, <coverage>), "runs" for SARIF, a first TN: or SF: line for lcov
--lowest <n>How many of the lowest-covered files to list (default 10, up to 1000)

Over MCP the tool is util_report, with file or text, format and lowest.

Output: { format, formatFrom, tests, findings, coverage, skipped, verified }. formatFrom is content or flag. One of tests, findings and coverage is filled in, by format, and the other two are null.

  • tests (JUnit, TRX): { suites, totals: { tests, passed, failures, errors, skipped, flaky, other }, failures: [{ suite, name, className, kind, type, message, file, line, location, stack, stackLines }] }. The totals are recounted from the cases, never copied from the report. kind is failure or error. stack is the first 15 lines, and stackLines how many there were. location is report when the report states file or line, and stack when they were read from the first stack frame naming the test’s class or method (an APPROXIMATED warning says how many). It’s null when neither has one.
  • findings (SARIF): { runs: [{ tool, version, results }], total, byLevel, results: [{ tool, rule, level, kind, file, line, message, suppressed }] }. level follows the spec: the result’s own, else its rule’s default, else warning for a failing result and none for any other. file is the first location’s URI as written, and line its startLine.
  • coverage (lcov, Cobertura): { sources, totals: { lines, branches }, files: [{ file, lines, branches }], lowest }. Each figure is { covered, total, percent }, with percent rounded to two places (null when there’s nothing to cover). branches is null where the report has no branch data. lowest lists the --lowest files with the lowest line coverage, leaving out files with no lines.
  • skipped: { count, elements: [{ element, count, reason }] }, every element (or lcov record) the reader met and didn’t read, also warned as REPORT_ELEMENTS_SKIPPED. Known parts that hold nothing it summarises (system-out, properties, TRX’s settings and lists, Cobertura’s per-method copies of the lines) aren’t counted.

What verified checks:

FormatCheckWarning when it fails
JUnitEach suite’s (and <testsuites>’) declared tests, failures, errors and skipped, recounted from its cases, nested suites includedREPORT_TOTALS_MISMATCH, naming both numbers
TRX<Counters>’ total and each outcome counter, recounted from the results’ outcomeREPORT_TOTALS_MISMATCH
CoberturaEvery stated line-rate and branch-rate (class, package and root), to within one unit of its last written decimal, and the root’s lines-covered, lines-valid, branches-covered and branches-validREPORT_COVERAGE_MISMATCH
lcovEach record’s LF, LH, BRF, BRH, FNF and FNH, recounted from its DA, BRDA, FN and FNDA linesREPORT_COVERAGE_MISMATCH
SARIFEach ruleIndex points at the rule its ruleId namesREPORT_SARIF_INCONSISTENT
AllThe whole input was read (input.complete)INPUT_INCOMPLETE, or INPUT_TRUNCATED at the cap

What it can’t check is reported as UNVERIFIED, never as passed: a JUnit report that declares no totals, SARIF (which declares none), a TRX counter left at 0 over results with that outcome (VSTest leaves notExecuted at 0, for one), and the size of stdin. TRX’s executed isn’t compared, because writers disagree on what it counts.

Formats it reads:

  • JUnit: Maven Surefire’s, the Jenkins shape (nested <testsuite>s, status, assertions, disabled) and the Azure DevOps shape (the VSTest JUnit logger’s). Surefire’s flakyFailure and flakyError mean a rerun passed: the case counts as passed and in flaky. A case with <error> is an error, else one with <failure> is a failure, else one with <skipped> is skipped.
  • TRX: dotnet test --logger trx and Visual Studio’s. Top-level results are counted, as the counters count them, and a data-driven test’s inner rows aren’t. failures is Failed; errors is Error, Timeout and Aborted; skipped is NotExecuted and NotRunnable; any other outcome is other. suites is the number of test classes, and a failure’s suite is its class.
  • SARIF 2.1.0: any tool’s. A rule reference with a toolComponent index is looked up in that entry of tool.extensions (CodeQL query packs); one that names its component only by guid can’t be found, so sarif.ruleIndex is UNVERIFIED and the level falls back to warning. A file with another version is read as 2.1.0, with an APPROXIMATED warning. A run whose invocation says it failed warns REPORT_TOOL_FAILED.
  • lcov: SF to end_of_record records, including lcov 2’s FNL and FNA. FNH is recounted as distinct functions hit: FNA by index, so a function’s aliases count once, and FNDA by name. A file in several records is merged, and a line is covered when any record hit it.
  • Cobertura: coverlet’s, coverage.py’s and others’. Classes in the same file are added together, and branch counts come from condition-coverage="50% (1/2)".

Limits: XML and lcov stream, so memory stays flat for a report of any size, apart from the failures it lists, up to the 64 MiB input cap. At the cap the read stops, INPUT_TRUNCATED says so, input.complete fails, and what came before the cut is summarised; a suite the cut left open isn’t compared. SARIF is JSON and is read whole, so a SARIF file over the cap is INVALID_INPUT. Malformed XML or JSON is INVALID_INPUT with the line and column. So is a document whose format can’t be detected, or whose root doesn’t match --format, with a fix naming --format.

toil util log

Triages a large log (a CI console, a Maven, npm or dotnet build, a test run) into what’s worth reading: its error and warning lines grouped by signature, each with the stack trace that follows it. It reads the file only, streams it, and holds memory constant however large the log is.

toil util log build.log
toil util log console.log --level error --context 3
toil util log console.log --since 2026-10-14T09:12:00Z --grep 'Failed to execute'
some-build 2>&1 | toil util log -
Argument or flagMeaning
[file]The log, inside the workspace. -, or no file and no --text, reads stdin
--text <text>The log itself, instead of a file
--since <timestamp>Only lines dated at or after this ISO 8601 time (2026-10-14, 2026-10-14T09:12:00Z, "2026-10-14 09:12:00"). A line with no date takes the date of the last dated line before it. Without a zone, a time is read as UTC
--level <level>warning (default) reports errors and warnings; error reports errors only
--grep <regex>Only error and warning lines matching this JavaScript regular expression (case-sensitive, no slashes or flags). An error also matches when the exception line heading its trace does (--grep IllegalStateException). Frames aren’t searched; LOG_GREP_STACK_ONLY says when only they matched
--max-groups <n>The most groups to return, default 50, up to 1000
--context <n>Lines to show before and after each group’s sample, default 0, up to 20

Over MCP the tool is util_log, with file (a path in the workspace) or text, and the same fields: since, level, grep, maxGroups, context.

How it reads a log:

  • Timestamps: a leading timestamp, bracketed (Jenkins’ timestamper) or bare (CI runners, log4j, Serilog), is set aside before anything else, so it never splits a group.
  • Levels: the first level word decides (ERROR, FATAL, SEVERE, WARN, WARNING, INFO, DEBUG …, and npm’s npm error / npm warn). A line tagged INFO, or with no tag, is still an error by its shape: BUILD FAILURE, FAILED, error CS0246:, error TS2322:, TypeError: …, Unhandled exception., an eslint or vstest failure line. A tag with nothing after it ([ERROR] ) is not a group.
  • Signatures: dates and times, UUIDs, hex and every number are replaced, and spaces collapsed. Codes such as CS0246 and TS2322 keep their digits, and paths and quoted names stay, so two different errors stay apart.
  • Stack traces: Java (at …(File.java:12), Caused by:, ... 14 more), .NET (at … in file:line 9, --->, --- End of inner exception stack trace ---), Node (at fn (file:12:3)) and Python (Traceback (most recent call last):, printed before its exception) are joined to the error they belong to, with the exception line that heads one. An exception line joins an error, never a warning: after a warning it’s an error of its own. A trace is reported for each group’s first occurrence, up to 50 lines.

Output:

{
  "lines": { "total": 76, "error": 20, "warning": 5, "other": 35, "stack": 12, "unclassified": 4 },
  "matched": 25, "filtered": 0, "groupsTotal": 18, "truncated": false, "ungrouped": 0, "unjoinedFrames": 0,
  "groups": [{
    "level": "error",
    "signature": "[ERROR] /build/ledger/Reconciler.java:[<n>] cannot find symbol",
    "count": 4, "firstLine": 27, "lastLine": 52,
    "sample": "[ERROR] /build/ledger/Reconciler.java:[54,38] cannot find symbol",
    "trace": { "kind": "java", "firstLine": 57, "lastLine": 68, "frames": 12, "lines": ["…"] },
    "context": { "before": [{ "line": 26, "text": "…" }], "after": [{ "line": 28, "text": "…" }] }
  }],
  "verified": { "passed": true, "checks": [{ "check": "lines.reread", "status": "passed", "checked": 36, "failed": 0 }] }
}

Groups are errors first, then warnings, each in order of first appearance. lines classes every line once: other is a level below warning, stack a trace line, and unclassified a line with no level at all. filtered counts the error and warning lines --since, --level or --grep left out.

It checks its own answer, in data.verified:

  • lines.reread: every group’s first line is read again from the file and must be its sample, and its last line must still have its signature. trace.reread does the same for every trace line shown. A mismatch is LOG_LINE_MISMATCH, which usually means the file changed while it was read.
  • groups.sum, lines.sum, filter.sum: the group counts add up to the matched lines, the line classes to the lines read, and matched plus filtered to the error and warning lines. A mismatch is LOG_COUNT_MISMATCH.
  • input.complete: the bytes read equal the file’s size. It’s unchecked for stdin and text.

What it reports in meta.warnings rather than leave out: LOG_UNCLASSIFIED (lines with no level, in no group), LOG_GROUPS_TRUNCATED (more groups than --max-groups), LOG_UNGROUPED (matched lines whose signature came after the first 2,000 distinct ones, counted but not grouped, which is what keeps memory constant), LOG_TRACE_UNJOINED (trace lines with no error before them), LOG_GREP_STACK_ONLY (--grep matched only stack trace lines), LOG_SINCE_UNDATED (lines --since couldn’t date, kept), and APPROXIMATED for a line longer than 4,096 characters (grouped by its start) or a --since compared with times that had no zone.

A file streams with no size limit. stdin and --text are held in memory, up to 64 MiB, so pass a file for anything bigger.

toil util size

How big a file or folder is before you read it, so an agent can budget its context: bytes, lines and an estimated token count, and for one file an outline with line ranges, so you can read just the part you need.

toil util size src/areas/util/size.ts
toil util size src --depth 2 --top 5
git show HEAD:README.md | toil util size - --language markdown
Argument / flagMeaning
[file]A file or folder inside the workspace. - (or nothing) reads stdin
--text <text>The content itself, instead of a file
--language <language>Outline it as this language: typescript, javascript, python, csharp, java, go, markdown, json or yaml. Needed for stdin and --text; for a file it overrides the extension
--top <n>For a folder: how many of the largest files to list (default 10)
--depth <n>For a folder: how many levels of subfolders the tree shows (default 3). Deeper folders still count in their parent’s totals, and foldersHidden says how many were left out

Tokens are an estimate: ceil(characters / 4) per file, counting Unicode code points. No model’s tokenizer is bundled, and real counts vary by model and content. Every result says so in tokenMethod and with an APPROXIMATED warning.

For a file: { kind: "file", path, language, bytes, lines, tokens, tokenMethod, outline, notOutlined, verified }. outline is { precision, method, symbols }, each symbol { name, kind, startLine, endLine, container } (headings add level):

  • Code (precision: "syntactic"): TypeScript and JavaScript (.ts, .tsx, .mts, .cts, .js, .jsx, .mjs, .cjs), Python, C#, Java and Go. Functions, classes, interfaces, types, enums, namespaces, methods, constructors, C# properties and exported names. It’s a pure-JavaScript scan that skips comments and strings and matches braces (indentation for Python), not a compiler, so method says what each language covers. Function bodies aren’t searched, and fields aren’t listed. container is the enclosing class or namespace.
  • Markdown: ATX and setext headings, outside code fences and front matter.
  • JSON and YAML (precision: "parsed"): the top-level keys, found by scanning and held against what the parser returns.

When there’s no outline, outline is null and notOutlined says why: binary (a NUL byte in the first 8,000 bytes; lines and tokens are null too), unsupported-language, parse-error (with the line, never the text; also a SIZE_PARSE_ERROR warning) or too-large (over 8 MiB; it’s still counted).

For a folder: { kind: "folder", path, tokenMethod, totals, tree, largest, skipped, verified }. It lists files the way deps scan does, skipping what .gitignore ignores. totals and every tree node hold files, bytes, lines, tokens and binaryFiles; binary files count in files and bytes only. Folders are sorted largest first. largest names the biggest files with their language. skipped lists what wasn’t counted, with the reason: unreadable (with a SIZE_FILES_SKIPPED warning), not-a-file or nested-repository.

What it checks, in data.verified:

  • outline.start: each symbol’s start line, re-read from the input, names it.
  • outline.range and outline.nesting: each range is inside the file and in order, and a member sits inside its container.
  • outline.keys: JSON and YAML keys match the parser’s.
  • counts.reread: the outline’s full read gives the same bytes and lines.
  • totals.sum and tree.sum: the totals equal the files added up, and each folder equals its own files plus its subfolders.
  • input.complete: every file was read to its size on disk.

A failed check sets verified.passed to false and warns SIZE_OUTLINE_MISMATCH, SIZE_TOTALS_MISMATCH or SIZE_COUNTS_MISMATCH.

Time: toil util time

Date and time arithmetic on the time zone data Node ships (IANA, through Intl); toil bundles no zone database of its own, and nothing reads the network. Each command checks its own answer a second way and reports the checks in data.verified ({ passed, checks }), with anything it couldn’t check or had to approximate in meta.warnings as UNVERIFIED or APPROXIMATED.

Times are ISO 8601: a date (2026-03-08), a wall clock (2026-03-08T02:30), or an instant with Z or an offset (2026-03-08T07:30:00Z, 2026-03-08T02:30:00-05:00). @1760000000 is epoch seconds, and now is the current time, read once per call. Fields out of range (2026-02-29, 24:00, a leap second) are INVALID_INPUT, never rolled over. Digits below a millisecond are dropped with an APPROXIMATED warning. Zones are IANA names (America/New_York); an unknown one is INVALID_INPUT.

DST. A wall clock a zone skipped (spring forward) or showed twice (fall back) is always reported, in data as a dst object and in meta.warnings as TIME_DST_GAP or TIME_DST_OVERLAP. A gap is read as the time the clocks showed after the jump (02:30 becomes 03:30) and an overlap as the earlier of the two. Give the time an offset to choose otherwise.

toil util time convert

toil util time convert 2026-03-08T02:30 --zone America/New_York --to UTC --to Europe/London
toil util time convert now --to Asia/Kolkata
Argument or flagMeaning
<time>The time to convert
--zone <zone>The zone of a time written without an offset. Required for one; refused for a time that has an offset
--to <zone>A zone to convert to (repeatable; default UTC)

Output: { input, instant, epochMs, source: { kind, zone, offset, dst? }, results: [{ zone, local, offset, offsetSeconds, dst? }], verified }. local is the time in that zone with its offset. Checks: each result reads back as the same instant (convert.roundtrip), the zone shows that wall clock then (convert.zone), and a wall-clock input is what its zone shows at the instant found (convert.source). A failure warns TIME_ROUNDTRIP_MISMATCH.

toil util time duration

toil util time duration P1DT2H30M
toil util time duration --seconds 93784.5
Argument or flagMeaning
<duration>An ISO 8601 duration to read: PT1H30M, P1Y2M10DT2H, PT0.5S, -PT15M. Only the last part may have a fraction
--seconds <seconds>Instead, a number of seconds to write as a duration

Output: { input, iso, negative, parts: { years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds }, totalSeconds, text, verified }. iso is the canonical text. Seconds are written in hours, minutes and seconds only (PT26H3M4.5S), since a day isn’t always 24 hours. Years and months have no fixed length, so totalSeconds is null with an UNVERIFIED warning; days and weeks count as 24 hours and 7 days, with an APPROXIMATED warning. Check: the canonical text reads back as the same parts (duration.roundtrip, warning DURATION_ROUNDTRIP_MISMATCH).

toil util time business-days add and diff

toil util time business-days add 2026-12-23 3 --holidays holidays-2026.txt
toil util time business-days add 2026-12-28 -1
toil util time business-days diff 2026-12-24T15:00 2026-12-29T10:00 --zone America/Chicago --holiday 2026-12-25
Argument or flagMeaning
<start>The start time or date
<days>add: business days to add; negative subtracts
<end>diff: the end time or date
--zone <zone>The zone whose calendar days count, and the zone of a time without an offset (default UTC)
--holidays <file>A file in the workspace: one YYYY-MM-DD per line, optionally followed by a name; # lines are comments. Any other line is INVALID_INPUT naming it
--holiday <date>A holiday as YYYY-MM-DD (repeatable)

Business days are Monday to Friday, less the holidays given. No country’s holidays are built in: list the dates the office is actually shut (the observed Friday, not the Saturday it stands in for).

add counts as a spreadsheet’s WORKDAY does: the start never counts, each step lands on the next business day, and 0 returns the start unchanged. A time of day is kept, and a result in a DST gap or overlap is warned about. Output: { start, days, zone, result, weekday, skipped: { weekendDays, holidays }, holidaysListed, dst?, verified }. Checks: the business days between start and result, counted again day by day, number days (business.count); the result is a business day (business.landing); and it’s on the right side of the start (business.direction). A failure warns BUSINESS_DAYS_MISMATCH.

diff measures the time between two times that falls on business days in the zone. A date means midnight. Output: { start, end, zone, negative, businessDays, hours, duration, totalBusinessSeconds, elapsedSeconds, holidays, verified }: businessDays is whole 24-hour days of business time, hours what’s left over, and duration the same, exactly (PT43H). DST days count as the 23 or 25 hours they are. Checks: business time plus the rest adds up to the elapsed time (business.partition), and the days and hours make the business time (business.total), warning BUSINESS_TIME_MISMATCH.

toil util time cron

toil util time cron "*/15 9-17 * * 1-5" --zone Europe/London --count 10
toil util time cron "0 0 12 ? * MON#2" --dialect quartz
toil util time cron "H H(0-7) * * 1-5" --dialect jenkins --job platform/api-build
Argument or flagMeaning
<expression>The cron expression, quoted
--dialect <dialect>standard, quartz or jenkins (default: detected: 6 or 7 fields is quartz, an H is jenkins, otherwise standard)
--zone <zone>The zone the schedule runs in (default UTC)
--from <time>List runs after this time (default now)
--count <n>How many run times to list, 1 to 100 (default 5)
--job <name>The Jenkins job’s full name (folder/job), which H is hashed from. Required when the expression uses H

The dialects:

  • standard: five fields, minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, as the classic crontab reads them. Names (JAN, MON), ranges, lists and steps (*/15, 1-30/5, 5/15); day-of-week 0 to 7, with 0 and 7 both Sunday. Macros @yearly, @annually, @monthly, @weekly, @daily, @midnight and @hourly; @reboot is refused, since it has no times. When neither day field starts with *, a day matching either runs. A detected standard expression with both day fields set warns CRON_DIALECT_ASSUMED, since Jenkins reads it differently.
  • quartz: six or seven fields, second first and an optional year (1970 to 2099) last. Day-of-week is 1 to 7 from Sunday. One of the day fields must be ?. Day-of-month takes L, L-3, 15W (the weekday nearest the 15th, inside the month) and LW; day-of-week takes 6L (the last Friday) and 6#3 (the third Friday). A backwards range wraps (FRI-MON, 22-2).
  • jenkins: five fields like standard, plus H, H(0-7) and H/15, placed as Jenkins places them from the job’s full name. An unbounded H in day-of-month stays within 1 to 28. Both day fields must match. The macros use H (@daily is H H * * *, @midnight is H H(0-2) * * *), so pass --dialect jenkins for a Jenkins macro: a bare macro is detected as standard.

Output: { expression, dialect, dialectSource, zone, from, explanation, fields, runs: [{ instant, local, offset, dst? }], skipped, skippedTotal, verified }. fields holds what each field expanded to, with day-of-week 0 for Sunday in every dialect.

DST: a run time the zone skipped isn’t listed as a run; it’s in skipped, with a CRON_DST_GAP warning giving the total. skipped lists the first 100 and skippedTotal counts them all. The walk stops after 5,000 skipped run times (more than one every-second gap hour), warning CRON_SEARCH_STOPPED with the last one reached, so a schedule that only lands in gaps (* * 2 ? 3 1#2 in New York) answers at once; pass a later --from to look further. A run time that happened twice is listed once, at the first, with a dst object and a CRON_DST_OVERLAP warning. Schedulers differ on both, so check yours. Fewer runs than --count in the next 100 years (or in Quartz’s listed years) warns CRON_FEW_RUNS; 0 0 30 2 * never runs.

Checks: each run, read back as the wall clock its zone shows then, matches every field again (cron.rematch); the runs come after --from and in order (cron.order); local is the same instant (cron.local); and each skipped time really is in a gap (cron.gap). A failure warns CRON_RUN_MISMATCH. The explanation’s wording isn’t checked, and says so (UNVERIFIED): it’s built from the same fields the run times come from, and the run times are what’s checked.

toil util md

Converts a document between Markdown and the rich-text formats the Atlassian areas send: Jira wiki markup (Jira Data Center), Atlassian Document Format (Jira Cloud, Confluence Cloud) and Confluence storage format (Confluence Data Center). One side is always Markdown. Every result is checked by converting it back, so you’re told exactly what didn’t survive.

toil util md description.md --to wiki
toil util md page.md --to storage
toil util md description.md --to adf --select output
toil util md PROJ-142.wiki --from wiki
toil util md description.adf.json --from adf

ADF input is the document itself, { "type": "doc", "version": 1, "content": [...] }: an issue’s fields.description or a comment’s body, not the issue around it.

Argument / flagMeaning
[file]A file inside the workspace. -, or no file and no --text, reads stdin
--text <text>The document itself, instead of a file
--to <format>wiki, adf or storage, to convert Markdown into it
--from <format>wiki, adf or storage, to convert it into Markdown

Over MCP the tool is util_md, with file or text plus from or to.

Output:

{
  "from": "md",
  "to": "wiki",
  "output": "h2. Steps\n\n# Open the login page\n...",
  "lossless": false,
  "losses": [{ "construct": "task list", "at": "line 12", "detail": "Jira wiki markup has no task lists; each task is written as [ ] or [x] text" }],
  "roundTrip": { "blocks": 9, "differences": [] },
  "verified": { "passed": true, "checks": [{ "check": "roundTrip.blocks", "status": "passed", "checked": 9, "failed": 0 }] }
}
  • output is the converted document: an ADF document object for adf, text for the others. Markdown output is in one canonical spelling (- bullets, *emphasis*, **strong**, fenced code, one line per paragraph).
  • losses lists every construct that has no equivalent in the target, with its position: line N in Markdown, wiki markup and storage format, a JSON pointer (/content/6/content/2) in ADF. Each kind is also an MD_LOSSY warning. Words are kept wherever there are words to keep: a panel becomes a quote, a mention becomes @name text, a merged cell is unmerged with the cells it covered left empty.
  • roundTrip: the output is read back and compared with the input, block by block, as canonical Markdown. differences shows each block that changed, and whether a loss explains it. A change no loss explains fails the roundTrip.blocks check and warns MD_ROUNDTRIP_MISMATCH: that’s a bug in the converter, so check the output before you send it.
  • lossless is true only when nothing was lost and every block came back the same.
  • ADF output is validated against the ADF JSON schema (Atlassian’s @atlaskit/adf-schema, bundled) before it’s returned, and storage output is read back as XML. Output that fails either is never returned; the command fails instead. ADF input the schema refuses is converted as far as it reads, with an ADF_INPUT_INVALID warning.

What Markdown means here: CommonMark plus GFM tables, task lists, strikethrough and bare-URL links. Raw HTML (other than <br>), link reference definitions and footnotes aren’t read; they’re kept as text and reported as losses.

Known losses, by format:

  • Wiki markup: no task lists (written as [ ] / [x] text), no table alignment, no link or image titles, lists always start at 1, and a list item is one line, so a code block or second paragraph in one is joined with line breaks. Underline, colour, sub/superscript, citations, panels, mentions, attachments and other macros don’t come back into Markdown. Text such as (y) that Jira shows as an emoticon, and a URL written as text, which Jira links, are reported too.
  • ADF: a quote can’t hold a heading, table, task list or another quote, and a list item can’t hold a heading, quote or table, so those are brought down and reported. Inline images become links; explicit left alignment is the default. Panels, expands, mentions, emoji, dates, statuses, smart links, decisions, attachments, layouts, extensions and merged cells don’t come back.
  • Storage format: a list mixing tasks and ordinary items becomes a task list. Info, note, tip and warning panels, expand, layouts, page and user links, attachments, emoticons, colour, merged cells and other macros don’t come back. Only XML’s entities and HTML’s common named ones (&nbsp;, &mdash; and so on) are read; any other is refused with INVALID_INPUT, as is XML that isn’t well-formed, with its line and column.

To send the result, pass it to the area’s own command: wiki markup as toil jira create-issue --description, storage format as toil confluence create-page --body (or confluence-cloud), and ADF as fields.description in a toil jira-cloud create-issue --input-file. How each product’s own renderer displays it hasn’t been checked against a live instance.

Commands at a glance

  • toil utiljwt decodealso toil jwt decode

    Decode a JWT token and output header, payload, and signature as JSON

    MCP util_jwt_decode<token>

  • toil utildeps scanalso toil deps scan

    Inventory all dependencies from manifest files (local only, no network)

    MCP util_deps_scan--ecosystem <ecosystem>--include-transitive--include-dev

  • toil utildeps diffalso toil deps diff

    Show dependency changes between two git refs (local only, no network)

    MCP util_deps_diff--from <ref>--to <ref>--ecosystem <ecosystem>--include-dev

  • toil utilencode

    Encode or decode base64, base64url, hex or URL text, or hash a file, and check the result

    MCP util_encode<scheme>[file]--text <text>--decode--out <file>

  • toil utilcert

    Decode certificates (PEM or DER, one or a chain) and check the chain order, signatures, validity and an optional host (local only, no network)

    MCP util_cert[file]--text <text>--host <host>

  • toil utilreport

    Summarise a JUnit, TRX, SARIF, lcov or Cobertura report as one JSON result, checked against its own totals (local only, no network)

    MCP util_report[file]--text <text>--format <format>--lowest <n>

  • toil utillog

    Triage a large log into grouped errors and warnings, with counts, line numbers, samples and stack traces

    MCP util_log[file]--text <text>--since <timestamp>--level <level>--grep <regex>--max-groups <n>--context <n>

  • toil utilsecrets scan

    Find credential-shaped strings in a file, folder, stdin or the staged diff (local only; exit 1 on findings)

    MCP util_secrets_scan[path]--text <text>--diff <kind>--allow-file <file>

  • toil utilsize

    Count bytes, lines and estimated tokens for a file or folder, and outline a file (local only)

  • toil utiltime convert

    Convert a time between time zones, reporting DST gaps and overlaps

  • toil utiltime duration

    Read an ISO 8601 duration, or write a number of seconds as one

  • toil utiltime business-days add

    Add or subtract business days, skipping weekends and listed holidays

    MCP util_time_business_days_add<start><days>--zone <zone>--holidays <file>--holiday <date>

  • toil utiltime business-days diff

    The business time between two times, in business days and hours

    MCP util_time_business_days_diff<start><end>--zone <zone>--holidays <file>--holiday <date>

  • toil utiltime cron

    Explain a cron expression and list its next run times in a zone

  • toil utilsemver compare

    Compare two versions and name the part they differ in (local only, no network)

    MCP util_semver_compare<a><b>--ecosystem <ecosystem>

  • toil utilsemver sort
